alt: Falling birth rates and rising life expectancy create an ageing population, which produces beanpole families and more care for elderly relatives; later parenthood makes the sandwich generation more likely. Below, a wide two-generation family tree contrasts with a long, thin four-generation beanpole.
caption: Birth and death trends are causes; the beanpole family is the effect.

alt: Three accounts across pre-industrial, early industrial and later industrial times. Parsons: extended family gives way to the isolated nuclear family. Laslett: pre-industrial households were already mostly nuclear; Anderson: extended households were common in Preston in 1851. Young and Willmott: from a family working together, to separate lives, to the symmetrical family.
caption: The shift from extended to nuclear was not as simple as Parsons claimed.

after: ## Explaining trends in marriage, divorce and cohabitation (4.3.3)
alt: Six explanations around the trends of fewer and later marriages and more divorce and cohabitation: legislation, changing attitudes, the internet, secularisation, cultural expectations, and the changing status and power of women.
caption: Name the factor, then explain how it changes behaviour.

alt: Three generations stacked: middle-aged adults in the middle care for their ageing parents above and their own children below at the same time.
caption: Longer lives and later parenthood squeeze the middle generation from both sides.

alt: Children have moved from economic asset to burden, families are more child-centred, and boomerang children return home. Grandparents provide childcare, economic support and advice but may become dependent. Conjugal roles have become more joint, though feminists point to the dual burden.
caption: Roles have changed for every generation in the family.
